analysis.one_liner: Bolsters family tax credits and paid parental leave while steering pregnancy-support money away from abortion providers.
analysis.headline: Rubio's family-support bill drew no cosponsors and never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the child tax credit to $3,500 per child ($4,500 for children under six) and make the adoption tax credit refundable. It would let new parents draw up to three months of Social Security payments for paid leave, with the money repaid later through smaller retirement benefits or a later retirement age. It would extend WIC benefits for new mothers from one year to two and require fathers to cover at least half of a mother's pregnancy and delivery out-of-pocket costs. To pay for part of it, the bill would eliminate the federal deduction for state and local taxes, and it would steer $100 million a year in grants plus a federal resource website toward pregnancy centers and mentoring programs that do not provide, refer for, or counsel in favor of abortion.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income families with children would get a larger child tax credit; new parents would get three months of payments drawn from Social Security; adoptive parents would get a refundable credit; pregnant and postpartum women would get a longer WIC eligibility period. Pregnancy resource centers and faith-based social-service organizations would gain new federal funding streams and a federal website that refers women to them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with children; anti-abortion pregnancy centers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the child tax credit to a maximum of $3,500 per child and $4,500 per child under six, and makes refundable a portion based on 15.3% of earned income, which matters most to families who owe little or no income tax.
Creates a paid parental leave benefit of up to three months paid at the rate of an early-retirement Social Security benefit, applied for through the Social Security Administration.
Makes the adoption tax credit refundable so adoptive families who owe less tax than the credit amount can still receive the full value.
Extends postpartum WIC eligibility from one year to two years after childbirth.
Requires states to enforce a child support obligation making biological fathers pay at least 50% of a mother's reasonable out-of-pocket pregnancy and delivery medical expenses at her request.
Authorizes $100 million a year for community-based maternal mentoring programs and requires public colleges to notify pregnant students of their rights and available resources.

analysis.who_pays: The bill repeals the federal deduction for state and local taxes, which would raise taxes for itemizers, concentrated among higher-income households in high-tax states. Parents who take the leave benefit must repay its full cost through reduced old-age benefits (up to 60 monthly deductions) or a later retirement age. SNAP recipients would face a new mandatory requirement to cooperate with child-support agencies; noncompliance could cost a family food benefits. Abortion providers would be barred from the new grants, the federal resource website, and the mentoring program.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners in high-tax states; abortion providers

drawbacks.text: The paid parental leave is not a free benefit: recipients must repay the full cost to the Social Security trust fund through deductions from their future retirement checks, up to 60 monthly payments, or by accepting a later retirement age, making it effectively an advance on their own retirement.
The bill eliminates the federal deduction for state and local taxes for all individuals, a tax increase concentrated on homeowners and higher earners in states with high state and local taxes.
It makes SNAP child-support cooperation mandatory for every state rather than optional, so a parent who does not cooperate risks losing food assistance.

All the new pregnancy-support funding, the mentoring grants, and the life.gov resource website exclude any entity that provides, refers for, or counsels in favor of abortion, and the website is required to present information on 'alternatives to abortion' and 'abortion risks' without listing abortion services — so women seeking abortion would be directed only to providers that do not offer it.

The bill gives religious organizations that receive federal social-service funds the right to retain religious hiring practices, limits federal audits to segregated accounts, preempts state and local laws that impose stricter conditions, and creates a private right of action with attorney's fees for religious organizations — a broad expansion of federal funding for religious providers that critics say comes at the expense of beneficiaries' protections.

The bill contains no identified funding source for the permanent child tax credit increase other than the SALT repeal, and the Congress's nonpartisan cost estimate was never produced because the bill received no committee action.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The family tax and benefit provisions are substantial and would deliver real money to working families — a bigger child credit, refundable adoption credit, and two years of WIC for new mothers. But the centerpiece paid-leave benefit is structured as a loan against the recipient's own retirement, the financing rests on a politically charged SALT repeal, and the bill builds a parallel pregnancy-support system that excludes abortion providers by law, meaning the money comes with conditions that only serve one side of a contested policy question. The bill also never received a cost estimate or a single hearing, so its full fiscal impact was never known.

outcome.mechanism: Marco Rubio introduced the bill in September 2022, the Senate referred it to the Finance Committee, no hearing or vote ever happened, and the Congress ended in January 2023 with the bill dead.

narrative.text: Sen. Marco Rubio introduced the Providing for Life Act in the Senate on September 15, 2022.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, where no further action was taken.
No other senator cosponsored the bill.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the bill receiving a committee markup, a floor vote, or a cost estimate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody enacted anything: families did not receive the proposed child credit increase or paid leave, while higher earners in high-tax states kept the SALT deduction and abortion providers were never excluded from federal programs. The pregnancy-center and religious-provider funding streams the bill would have created never materialized.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 15, 2022 and took no further action — no markup, hearing, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Pregnancy resource centers and anti-abortion counseling providers
industries.note: The bill would give them $100 million a year in mentoring and pregnancy-center grants, a dedicated federal resource website (life.gov), and hotline referrals — while legally excluding any competitor that provides, refers for, or counsels in favor of abortion. For women who want to continue a pregnancy, the centers' free services run alongside their interest; for women seeking abortion, the funding structure steers them away from the full set of options.

The bill defines them as 'prohibited entities' barred from the mentoring grants, the federal resource website, the state resource lists, and the hotline, and colleges' pregnancy-resource notices must exclude abortion services.

A standalone section makes religious organizations eligible for federal social-service funding on equal terms, lets them keep religious hiring practices and symbols, limits audits to segregated federal-fund accounts, preempts state and local rules to the contrary, and gives them a private right of action with attorney's fees. This opens substantial new funding to them while loosening oversight and beneficiary protections relative to current law.

Repealing the federal deduction for state and local taxes raises their federal taxes; the bill treats this as a partial offset for the expanded child credit, which phases out above $200,000 for singles and $400,000 for joint filers.

The parental leave benefit draws on the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund but is fully repaid by recipients through reduced future retirement benefits or a later retirement age, so the trust fund is designed to be made whole; the mechanism shifts the cost onto the future retiree rather than the government.
